background.definition: High-altitude illness is used to describe a spectrum of syndromes that may develop in unacclimatized persons shortly after ascent to high altitudes including acute mountain sickness (AMS), high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE), and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE). The Lake Louise Consensus Group defines AMS as the presence of headache in an unacclimatized person who has recently arrived at an altitude of 2500 m (8202 ft), plus the presence of one or more of the following: GI symptoms (anorexia, nausea or vomiting), insomnia, dizziness, lassitude, or fatigue.

list.listitem: Incidence is equal in children and adults.
A meta-analysis of 18 prospective studies (n = 7669) suggested that incidence is higher in women than in men (RR=1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.41)
Prevalence rates range from 15% to 75% depending on the speed of ascent, the altitude reached, and individual susceptibility.

Prevalence rates differ at various altitudes and increase with the altitude reached. In the Swiss Alps, rates were 9% at 2850 m (9350 ft), 13% at 3050 m (10,007 ft), 34% at 3650 m (12,133 ft), and 53% at 4559 m (14,957 ft).
Twenty-five percent of recreational visitors to the Colorado mountains experience AMS at moderate elevations (6300-9700 ft).
Ascent to altitude, especially if ascent is too rapid.
The exact mechanism is unknown, although evidence points to a process involving the CNS.

Characteristics of established AMS include relative hypoventilation, impaired gas exchange, increased sympathetic activity, fluid retention and redistribution, and in moderate to severe AMS, raised intracranial pressure.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Residence at altitude of less than 900 m (2953 ft)

list.listitem: Patients with certain pre-existing conditions, such as obstructive sleep apnea, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, pulmonary hypertension, thromboembolic disease, and others should be screened and counseled about travel to high-altitude destinations prior to travel (see ). C
Above 2500 m (8202 ft), the altitude at which one sleeps should be no more than 600 m higher than the previous day, and a rest day should be added for acclimatization every 600 to 1200 m. C

If greater distances or faster rates of ascent are planned, prophylaxis with acetazolamide (250 to 750 mg daily) appears effective, A while the efficacy of dexamethasone, budesonide, and ibuprofen is uncertain. B

There is insufficient evidence for other pharmacologic interventions (e.g., sumatriptan, spironolactone, medroxyprogesterone, magnesium citrate), vitamins, and supplements (e.g., ginko biloba) in preventing AMS. B
In a small RCT, a slower ascent protocol (15 vs. 19 days to ascend 7546 m) reduced the incidence of AMS, AMS severity, and ascent success.
In an RCT of 343 healthy mountain trekkers, acetazolamide 85 mg and ibuprofen 600 mg had similar effectiveness in preventing AMS.
In an RCT of 138 healthy young men, inhaled budesonide and oral dexamethasone were both more effective than placebo in preventing AMS.However, another RCT found budesonide to be ineffective.

AMS is defined as the presence of headache in an unacclimatized person who has recently arrived at an altitude of 2500 m (8202 ft), plus the presence of one or more of the following: GI symptoms (anorexia, nausea, or vomiting), insomnia, dizziness, lassitude, or fatigue. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Ingestion of drugs, toxins, and alcohol

list.listitem: AMS is characterized by nonspecific symptoms and a paucity of physical findings. Main symptoms include headache, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, dizziness, and sleep disturbance.
Headache is deemed the cardinal symptom. Symptoms typically develop 6 to 12 hours after ascent.

There are different survey tools used to evaluate for AMS, but a commonly used tool is the Lake Louise Questionnare Score (LLQS). The Lake Louise Consensus Group defines AMS as the presence of headache in an unacclimatized person who has recently arrived at an altitude of 2500 m (8202 ft), plus the presence of one or more of the following: GI symptoms (anorexia, nausea, or vomiting), insomnia, dizziness, lassitude, or fatigue.

The Lake Louise Consensus Group scoring system assesses 5 symptom categories (headache, gastrointestinal upset, fatigue, dizziness, and sleep disturbance) on a scale from 0 to 3, where 0 = no symptoms and 1, 2, and 3 = mild, moderate, and severe symptoms, respectively. The magnitude of AMS is assessed on the following scale: 0 = no AMS; 1-5 = mild AMS; 6-9 = moderate AMS; >10 = severe AMS.

Another simple tool that can be used is called the Clinical Function Score (CFS). It asks a single question; "Overall, if you had any symptoms, how did they affect your activity?" It is scored on a scale of 0-3 (0 – no reduction in activity, 1 – mild reduction in activities, 2 – moderate reduction in activities, and 3 – severe reduction in activities). This tool could be used as a screening test and if the score was 2 or greater, then the patient would need the full Lake Louise Questionnaire.

The following suggest another diagnosis: onset of symptoms more than 3 days after arrival to given altitude; absence of headache; rapid response to fluids or rest; and absence of response to descent, oxygen, or dexamethasone.
AMS is a clinical diagnosis based on presence of symptoms.

Depending on the clinical presentation, consider further work-up to exclude other causes. For example, in a patient with headache and shortness of breath, consider chest x-ray, D-dimer, and/or oxygen saturation to rule out pneumonia or pulmonary embolus. In a patient with headache, nausea, and vomiting, consider viral or bacterial gastroenteritis or food poisoning.

Suspect AMS in an unacclimatized patient with headache who has recently arrived at an altitude of 2500 m (8202 ft) and also has at least one of the following: anorexia, nausea or vomiting, insomnia, dizziness, lassitude, or fatigue.
Rule out other diagnoses such as pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, gastroenteritis, or meningitis as clinically indicated.
Initial treatment is with oxygen and descent. If not contraindicated, acetazolamide, and/or dexamethasone are effective pharmacotherapies.
Descent and oxygen are the treatments of choice for AMS. Simulated descent with hyperbaric oxygen chambers is also effective. C
If oxygen is not available and descent is not possible, medical therapy may resolve symptoms. C
Acetazolamide is the recommended initial medical therapy for AMS. B
Dexamethasone may also effective in reducing the severity of AMS. B

Acetazolamide is the recommended initial medical therapy. Doses from 500 to 750 mg daily in divided doses have been studied. In a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs, the 750 mg dose was effective (typically given 250 mg by mouth thrice a day), but the 500 mg daily dose was not effective for the prevention of AMS. In a large subsequent study of 487 patients, though, a dose of 250 mg twice daily was effective.
Acetazolamide must be used cautiously in patients with COPD and renal insufficiency and should be avoided in those with hepatic disease, pregnancy, or sulfa allergy.

Dexamethasone is effective in reducing the severity of AMS in doses from 8 to 20 mg per day. It is a safe alternative to acetazolamide in patients with renal or hepatic disease. It should be avoided in pregnant patients and those with peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding and should be used with caution in diabetic patients. It may also cause depression if abruptly discontinued.
Low-dose theophylline (300 mg daily) reduced AMS symptoms in 1 small RCT.
In an RCT of 37 mountaineers, salmeterol by inhaler (125 mcg every 12 hours) reduced the likelihood of pulmonary edema (NNT = 2.4) and AMS.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 5 small RCTs of inhaled corticosteroids (n = 304) did not find a statistically significant preventive effect against AMS, but likely lacked adequate power to identify a difference in this outcome.

Several medicines have been studied in single trials to reduce specific symptoms associated with AMS including ibuprofen, gabapentin, zolpidem, and temazepam (see ). The efficacy of sumatriptan for treatment of high-altitude headache is uncertain.
In a recent RCT of gabapentin versus placebo, headache incidence was not significantly reduced (43.1% vs. 54.9%), but fewer patients experienced moderate or severe headache (26.5% vs. 41.2%).
Early, smaller studies had varying results for ginkgo, perhaps due to varying preparations and dosages of the herb.
A large double-blind RCT found that ginkgo biloba was ineffective either alone or in combination with acetazolamide for the prevention of AMS; it slightly increased the likelihood of headache.
Chachacoma tea and coca leaf chew have not been shown to decrease symptoms of AMS.
Oral antioxidant supplements do not prevent AMS.

Descent and oxygen are the treatments of choice for AMS. A descent of 500 to 1000 m (1640-3281 ft) usually results in resolution of symptoms. Simulated descent with hyperbaric oxygen chambers is also effective.
If oxygen is not available and descent is not possible, medical therapy may resolve symptoms (see and ).
AMS may be viewed as a spectrum of illnesses that ranges from mild to life threatening.

At the life-threatening end of this spectrum is HACE, which requires hospitalization. HACE is defined as symptoms of AMS plus gait ataxia or mental status changes. HACE may also be defined as gait ataxia and mental status changes regardless of AMS symptoms.

Another form of severe AMS usually requiring hospitalization is HAPE. HAPE is diagnosed in patients with at least two of the following signs and symptoms: dyspnea at rest, cough, weakness, decreased exercise performance, chest tightness or congestion and crackles, wheezing, central cyanosis, tachypnea, or tachycardia.
Approximately, half of the patients with HAPE also have AMS and 14% also have HACE.

feature.caption: Medical Management of Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS).
feature.feature_body:
Agent Dose Comments
Oxygen 2-4 L/min by cannula or mask initially, then 1-2 L/min or titrate until SaO2 >90% Works within minutes, improves headaches associated with AMS.
Portable hyperbaric chamber Depends on model; 2-4 psi for a minimum of 2 h, then may continue as needed Potential rebound effect after removal from chamber.
Acetazolamide Prevention: 250 mg PO bid to tid 24 h prior to ascent and for first 2 days at altitude Side effects include paresthesias, polyuria; alters taste of carbonated beverages. Adjust dose in renal disease and avoid with liver disease. In patients with COPD, limit dose to 125 mg bid or use dexamethasone. Use caution in those with sulfa allergy, contraindicated in pregnancy, and should be avoided with long-term high-dose aspirin therapy.
Treatment: 250 mg PO bid to tid until symptoms resolve
Pediatric 5 mg/kg PO divided doses every 8-12 h
Dexamethasone Prevention: 2 mg every 6 h or 4 mg every 12 h PO Side effects include mood changes, hyperglycemia, dyspepsia; may cause rebound effect on withdrawal. DOC with renal or hepatic disease. Caution with diabetes mellitus. Avoid with peptic ulcer disease or recent history of GI bleed. Avoid in amebiasis or strongyloidiasis. Effectiveness may be decreased with antiseizure medications.
Treatment: 4 mg every 6 h PO/IM/IV
Pediatric: 0.15 mg/kg every 6 h PO/IM/IV
PO denotes by mouth; bid, twice a day; tid, 3 times per day; IM, intramuscular; IV, intravenous; GI, gastrointestinal.

feature.caption: Treatment for Specific Symptoms Associated with Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS).
feature.feature_body:
Agent Indication Dose Comments
Aspirin Prevention of headache 325 mg PO every 4 h for a total of 3 doses Side effects include dyspepsia and GI bleeding. No clinical trials for treatment of AMS
Ibuprofen Treatment of headache 400 or 600 mg PO once, may be repeated Side effects include dyspepsia and GI bleeding. No clinical trials for prevention of AMS
Gabapentin1
Treatment of high-altitude headache 300 mg PO Few side effects. Preliminary study; larger RCTs needed
Temazepam2
Treatment of periodic breathing; improve sleep efficiency 10 mg PO every bedtime x 2 doses No adverse effect on next day reaction time; additional studies needed to confirm findings
Zolpidem3
Insomnia 10 mg PO every bedtime Rare side effects; short-acting; does not depress ventilation at high altitude. Pregnancy category B
Prochlorperazine Nausea; vomiting 10 mg PO/IM every 6-8 h Extrapyramidal reactions; causes sedation. Pregnancy category C
Promethazine Nausea; vomiting 25-50 mg PO/IM/PR every 6 h Extrapyramidal reactions; causes sedation. Pregnancy category C

feature.caption: Recommendations for Travel to High Altitude in Patients with Pre-existing Disease.
feature.feature_body:
COPD If FEV1 is <15 L, assess need for supplemental O2 and administer during stay at high altitude if predicted PaO2 is <50-55 mm Hg.
Evaluate for comorbid diseases that may also affect the response to altitude.
Continue baseline medications and carry supply of rescue inhalers and prednisone for potential exacerbations.
Asthma Patients with mild intermittent or mild persistent disease may ascend to altitudes as high as 5000 m (16,404 ft).
Caution patients with more severe disease against high-altitude travel.
Continue baseline medications and carry peak flow meter and supply of rescue inhalers and prednisone for potential exacerbations.
Consider using balaclava or bandana over mouth to warm and humidify air in cold environments.
Pulmonary hypertension Counsel patients against high-altitude travel.
If high-altitude travel cannot be avoided, counsel patients about the risks, symptoms, and signs of HAPE.
Administer supplemental oxygen for trips above 2000 m (6562 ft), even in patients not using supplemental oxygen at baseline.
For patients not using pre-existing medical therapy, use prophylactic nifedipine SR 20 mg bid.
Thrombo-embolic disease Continue any pre-existing anticoagulation regimen during high-altitude stay with close follow-up of INR before and after trip.
Discontinue oral contraceptives in women with pre-existing coagulopathy.
Avoid immobility and dehydration.
Obesity hypoventilation Counsel against high-altitude travel.
If high altitude-travel cannot be avoided, administer supplemental oxygen for day and nighttime use.
Counsel patients about the risks for and symptoms of AMS and provide prophylaxis with acetazolamide 125-250 mg bid.
In patients with pre-existing CPAP use, ensure patient travels to altitude with CPAP unit.
Obstructive and central sleep apnea Travel to altitude with CPAP machine.
For patients with central sleep apnea, consider acetazolamide 250 mg bid.
Continue pre-existing nocturnal oxygen therapy during high-altitude stay.
Evaluate patients with daytime hypoxemia for the presence of pulmonary hypertension and, if present, provide prophylaxis with nifedipine SR 20 mg bid.
Prior carotid artery surgery Avoid high-altitude travel in patients with preceding bilateral carotid resection.
If travel cannot be avoided, administer supplemental oxygen.
Assess hyperbaric ventilatory response in patients with prior history of carotid endarterectomy and administer supplemental oxygen if response is suppressed.
BID denotes twice a day; INR, international normalized ratio; CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure. Adapted from Luks AM, Swenson ER. Travel to high altitude with pre-existing lung disease. Eur Respir J 2007;29:770-792.
